title: Insula Atlas
subtitle: Map interoception, salience, taste and autonomic integration
altText: Chalkboard-style anatomical atlas illustration highlighting the insula atlas and its major connections.
learningObjectives: Identify the major components of the insula atlas.
Trace key connections and functional relationships of the insula atlas.
Relate lesions or network disruption to plausible clinical presentations.

sections.explainSimply: The insula is folded deep inside the lateral sulcus and helps integrate body signals with emotion, attention and action.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The insula supports interoception, salience detection and switching between internally and externally focused networks.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The insular cortex contains posterior-to-anterior gradients from primary interoceptive and somatosensory representations toward multimodal, affective and cognitive integration. It connects with thalamus, amygdala, cingulate, orbitofrontal cortex, striatum and brainstem autonomic centres.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A concealed control room that combines body telemetry with context before signalling what deserves attention.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Insular dysfunction can contribute to altered interoception, disgust processing, craving, pain, panic and salience attribution, but symptoms reflect network-level dysfunction rather than a single-region diagnosis.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt salience network, interoception, autonomic regulation; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: Do not equate strong bodily awareness or anxiety with an “overactive insula”; infer mechanisms cautiously.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses the insula atlas map to test whether a patient’s pattern is anatomically coherent while considering broader network and medical explanations.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas localisation supports hypothesis generation, not diagnosis. Individual anatomy, distributed processing, compensation and comorbidity limit one-to-one structure–symptom claims.

anatomy.position: Integrated within deep or medial cortical-brainstem relationships shown in the atlas.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the insula atlas?
options: The insula supports interoception, salience detection and switching between internally and externally focused networks.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

quiz.question: What is the safest clinical inference from this atlas?
options: A lesion pattern can guide hypotheses but requires clinical and medical correlation.
One symptom proves one structure is damaged.
quiz.rationale: Neuroanatomy constrains hypotheses but does not replace assessment.

quiz.question: Why are connections important?
options: Symptoms can reflect disconnection and downstream network effects.
All pathways are identical across people.
quiz.rationale: Distributed cognitive systems depend on pathways linking regions.
